lines.text:
From Dough to Delivery — The Art and Business of Pizza

Pizza is arguably the world's most universal food. It crossed the Atlantic from Naples in the late nineteenth century, adapted to local ingredients everywhere it landed, and became a global industry worth hundreds of billions of dollars. Yet at its core, pizza remains astonishingly simple: dough, sauce, and cheese — transformed by heat.

The process begins at the prep table. Dough is made from flour, water, yeast, salt, and olive oil. A mixer combines the ingredients. The dough rests, rises, and is portioned into balls. A rolling pin flattens each ball — though many pizzaioli prefer to stretch by hand, arguing that a rolling pin compresses the air bubbles that give the crust its texture. Flour prevents sticking.

Sauce is ladled onto the base with a ladle — typically a simple tomato sauce, sometimes with garlic and basil. Mozzarella is the standard cheese, grated or sliced. From here, the toppings define the pizza. A Margherita carries only tomato, mozzarella, and basil — the colours of the Italian flag. Pepperoni adds cured meat. A Hawaiian controversially combines pineapple and ham. A veggie pizza layers pepper, onion, olive, and mushroom. Meat Lovers piles sausage, pepperoni, bacon, and ground beef. A Four Cheese blends mozzarella, parmesan, gorgonzola, and ricotta. BBQ Chicken substitutes barbecue sauce for tomato. A Supreme combines everything. A calzone folds the dough over the filling into a sealed half-moon.

The oven is where chemistry becomes flavour. A brick oven — heated by wood or gas — reaches temperatures above four hundred degrees Celsius. A pizza stone distributes heat evenly. A pizza peel — a flat wooden or metal paddle — slides the pizza in and out. At these temperatures, the crust blisters and chars in minutes. A timer ensures consistency. A pizza cutter — a circular blade on a handle — divides the finished product into slices.

Service is fast. A slice is placed on a plate with a napkin. A shaker of chilli flakes and parmesan sits on the counter. Garlic bread and a salad complement the meal. Dipping sauce accompanies the crust. A soda is the traditional drink. The menu — displayed on a board or handed across the counter — lists every combination. A booth or a table and chair provide seating. A register processes payment.

Delivery extends the shop's reach. A phone takes orders. A ticket prints in the kitchen. The pizza is placed in a box, the box into a delivery bag — insulated to retain heat — and loaded onto a delivery bike. The driver navigates by smartphone.

The recipe is ancient. The format is universal. The variations are infinite. And the appeal — hot, shareable, customisable, affordable — has made pizza one of the few foods that every culture has adopted without resistance.

lines.text: In English, 'pepperoni' = spicy cured sausage (a pizza topping). In Italian, 'peperoni' = bell peppers (the vegetable). This causes confusion! If you order 'pepperoni' in Italy, you might get peppers, not sausage. The Italian word for the sausage is 'salame piccante'.

lines.text: UK/US pizza sizes: Personal (7-8 inches, 1 person), Small (10 inches, 1-2 people), Medium (12 inches, 2-3 people), Large (14 inches, 3-4 people). In Italy, each person usually orders their own pizza — sharing is less common.

lines.text: Takeaway vs Delivery vs Eat In
lines.name: Takeaway vs Delivery vs Eat In

lines.text: 'Takeaway' (BrE) = 'takeout' (AmE) = food you collect and eat elsewhere. 'Delivery' = food brought to your door. 'Eat in' (BrE) = 'dine in' (AmE) = eating at the restaurant. 'For here or to go?' is the classic American question.

lines.text: In the UK, tipping the delivery driver is appreciated but not required (£1-2 is typical). In the US, tipping the delivery driver 15-20% is standard and expected — drivers rely on tips as part of their income.

lines.text: 'Fewer' + countable plural: 'fewer toppings', 'fewer slices.' 'Less' + uncountable: 'less cheese', 'less sauce.' 'Toppings' are countable (you can count olives, peppers, mushrooms), so 'fewer' is correct. 'Cheese' is uncountable, so 'more cheese' and 'less cheese' are both correct.

lines.text: Linking verbs (smell, taste, look, feel, sound) take adjectives: 'smells delicious', 'tastes wonderful', 'looks perfect.' Adverbs follow action verbs: 'He sniffed the pizza hungrily' (action — how he sniffed). 'The pizza smells delicious' (linking — describes the pizza). Test: replace with 'is' — if the sentence still works, use an adjective.

lines.text: 'Tell' + person: 'told me that...' 'Say' + (to person): 'said (to me) that...' Never *'said me.' Pattern: 'He told the customer...' / 'He said to the customer...' / 'He said that...' The person is the direct object of 'tell' but the indirect object (with 'to') of 'say.'

lines.text: 'For' + duration: 'for two years', 'for six months', 'for a long time.' 'Since' + point in time: 'since 2024', 'since last January', 'since we moved here.' Never *'since two years' — that's a duration, not a starting point. Duration = 'for.' Starting point = 'since.'
